title: Filtration

stems.label: A
stems.text: Total filtration for medical X-ray equipment (excluding mammography) must be greater than 2.5 mm aluminium equivalent
stems.explanation: General radiographic equipment operating above 70 kV must have total filtration of at least 2.5 mm aluminium equivalent to remove low-energy photons that would only add to skin dose.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Lower filtration is used for CT compared with general radiography
stems.explanation: CT uses considerably heavier filtration than general radiography (typically several mm aluminium equivalent plus a shaped bow-tie filter) to harden the beam and reduce beam-hardening artefact.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Inherent filtration is 0.5 - 1 mm of aluminium equivalent
stems.explanation: The tube envelope, insulating oil and exit window together provide inherent filtration of roughly 0.5-1 mm aluminium equivalent; added filtration makes up the rest of the required total.

stems.label: D
stems.text: 0.1-0.5 mm of copper filtration may be added for specialist applications
stems.explanation: Copper filters of 0.1-0.5 mm (or more) are added in interventional and paediatric work to preferentially remove low-energy photons and reduce skin dose.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Total filtration for dental X-ray equipment must be greater than the equivalent of 2.5 mm aluminium
stems.explanation: Dental sets operating up to 70 kV require only 1.5 mm aluminium equivalent total filtration; the 2.5 mm requirement applies to equipment operating above 70 kV.

keyPoint: Total filtration must exceed 2.5 mm Al equivalent above 70 kV (1.5 mm for dental sets up to 70 kV); CT uses more filtration than radiography, not less.

title: The quantity of X-ray photons emitted from an X-ray tube

stems.label: A
stems.text: Depends upon the kVp used
stems.explanation: X-ray tube output (photon quantity) increases approximately with the square of the applied kVp, so kVp strongly affects quantity as well as quality.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Will be greater for a tungsten target than for a molybdenum target tube provided all other factors remain unchanged
stems.explanation: Bremsstrahlung production efficiency is proportional to the atomic number of the target, so tungsten (Z=74) yields more photons than molybdenum (Z=42) for the same tube settings.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Will be doubled if the kVp is increased from 60 to 85 kVp
stems.explanation: Output is roughly proportional to kVp squared: (85/60)^2 is approximately 2, so raising 60 kVp to 85 kVp about doubles the photon output.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Depends on the degree of filtration
stems.explanation: Filtration removes photons (especially low-energy ones) from the beam, so increasing filtration reduces the quantity of photons emerging from the tube assembly.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Depends on the distance between the anode and cathode
stems.explanation: The anode-cathode gap does not determine photon output; quantity is governed by mA, exposure time, kVp, target material and filtration.

keyPoint: X-ray output rises with mAs, target atomic number and approximately with kVp squared, and is reduced by filtration; tube geometry between electrodes is irrelevant.

title: With respect to radioactive decay processes

stems.label: A
stems.text: The activity of a radionuclide is 1 MBq if there are 1000 nuclear disintegrations per second
stems.explanation: 1 becquerel is one disintegration per second, so 1 MBq corresponds to one million disintegrations per second, not 1000.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The half-life is 0.693 multiplied by the decay constant
stems.explanation: The half-life equals 0.693 divided by the decay constant (T1/2 = ln2/lambda), not multiplied by it.

stems.label: C
stems.text: After 10 half-lives the activity of a radionuclide will have decreased by a little more than 1000-fold
stems.explanation: After 10 half-lives activity falls by a factor of 2^10 = 1024, i.e. slightly more than 1000-fold.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Different radioisotopes of the same element always have different half-lives
stems.explanation: The physical half-life is a characteristic property of each individual nuclide, so different isotopes of the same element have their own distinct half-lives.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The physical half-life is independent of the biological half-life in the body
stems.explanation: Physical decay is a property of the nucleus and proceeds regardless of biological excretion; the two combine to give the effective half-life.

keyPoint: 1 Bq = 1 disintegration per second, T1/2 = 0.693/lambda, and 10 half-lives reduce activity roughly 1000-fold (2^10 = 1024).

title: The quality of the X-ray spectrum emerging from an X-ray tube depends on

stems.label: A
stems.text: The peak voltage applied to the tube
stems.explanation: kVp sets the maximum and mean photon energies of the spectrum and is the main operator control of beam quality.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The waveform of the applied voltage
stems.explanation: Less voltage ripple (e.g. high-frequency generators) keeps the tube closer to peak potential, raising the mean photon energy and hence beam quality.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The atomic number of the anode
stems.explanation: Target atomic number determines the characteristic line energies and influences the bremsstrahlung spectrum, so it affects beam quality.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The angle of the anode
stems.explanation: Anode angle governs the effective focal spot size and heel-effect intensity distribution rather than the overall spectral quality of the beam.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The atomic number of the tube window
stems.explanation: The window contributes inherent filtration; a higher atomic number window absorbs more low-energy photons and hardens the beam.

keyPoint: Beam quality is set by kVp, voltage waveform, target material and filtration (including the tube window); anode angle mainly affects focal spot and heel effect.

title: In carrying out quality assurance checks on X-ray equipment

stems.label: A
stems.text: An ionisation chamber may be used to detect leakage radiation
stems.explanation: Leakage through the tube housing is measured with a suitable dosimeter such as an ionisation chamber positioned around the housing at 1 m.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Light beam alignment may be checked by imaging a rectangular metal frame
stems.explanation: Placing radio-opaque markers or a metal frame at the light-field edges and exposing a detector shows any misalignment between light and X-ray fields.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Total filtration may be estimated by measuring the half value thickness of aluminium for the beam
stems.explanation: Measuring the beam's HVL in aluminium at a known kVp allows the total filtration to be inferred from published HVL-filtration tables.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Intensifying screens may be checked using visible light
stems.explanation: Screens are routinely inspected under visible (and ultraviolet) light for dirt, damage and artefacts as part of QA.

stems.label: E
stems.text: A resolution of 2.0 line pairs per millimetre would be acceptable for a fluoroscopy system
stems.explanation: Fluoroscopy systems typically resolve around 1-2 lp/mm at the displayed image, so 2.0 lp/mm is acceptable performance for fluoroscopy.

keyPoint: QA uses ionisation chambers for leakage, HVL measurements to estimate filtration, and simple test objects for field alignment; fluoroscopy resolution of about 2 lp/mm is acceptable.

title: Signal to noise in an MRI is increased with

stems.label: A
stems.text: Shorter TE
stems.explanation: A shorter TE allows less T2/T2* decay before readout, so more transverse magnetisation remains and SNR is higher.

stems.label: B
stems.text: An increased matrix size
stems.explanation: Increasing the matrix at a fixed field of view makes voxels smaller, so each voxel contains less signal and SNR falls.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A larger field of view
stems.explanation: A larger FOV with the same matrix gives bigger voxels containing more spins, increasing SNR (at the cost of spatial resolution).

stems.label: D
stems.text: Use of a higher magnetic field
stems.explanation: Higher B0 increases net magnetisation and hence signal, giving approximately proportionally higher SNR.

stems.label: E
stems.text: A thicker slice
stems.explanation: Thicker slices increase voxel volume and the number of contributing spins, raising SNR at the expense of partial volume effects.

keyPoint: MRI SNR rises with anything that increases signal per voxel: larger voxels (bigger FOV, thicker slice, smaller matrix), shorter TE and higher field strength.

title: When X-rays interact with matter, the following statements are true

stems.label: A
stems.text: Absorption of X-radiation by the photoelectric effect results in annihilation of radiation
stems.explanation: Photoelectric absorption ejects an inner-shell electron with photon absorption; annihilation radiation arises from positron-electron interactions, not the photoelectric effect.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The photoelectric effect usually predominates over the Compton effect in X-ray computed tomography
stems.explanation: At the mean beam energies used in CT (about 60-70 keV), Compton scatter is the dominant interaction in soft tissue.

stems.label: C
stems.text: In the Compton effect the energy of the incident photon is shared between an electron and a scattered photon
stems.explanation: Compton interaction transfers part of the incident photon energy to a recoil electron, the remainder leaving as a scattered photon.

stems.label: D
stems.text: In the Compton effect the majority of photons are scattered backwards at the scattering centre at diagnostic energies
stems.explanation: At diagnostic energies Compton scatter is predominantly in the forward direction; backscatter is a minority of events.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Absorption of X-radiation by pair production is accompanied by the release of 1.02 MeV radiation
stems.explanation: The positron produced ultimately annihilates with an electron, releasing two 0.511 MeV photons totalling 1.02 MeV; pair production itself requires photons above 1.02 MeV and does not occur at diagnostic energies.

keyPoint: Compton scatter dominates in soft tissue at CT energies and is forward-peaked; pair production needs more than 1.02 MeV and ends in two 0.511 MeV annihilation photons.

title: The following dosimetric quantities are approximately correct

stems.label: A
stems.text: The effective dose from a barium enema is 7 mSv
stems.explanation: A barium enema is one of the highest-dose fluoroscopic contrast studies, with a typical effective dose of about 7 mSv.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The annual whole body effective dose limit for members of the public is 15 mSv
stems.explanation: The annual effective dose limit for a member of the public is 1 mSv; 15 mSv is the public equivalent-dose limit for the lens of the eye.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A chest X-ray entrance skin dose is 150 µGy
stems.explanation: A PA chest radiograph has an entrance surface dose of roughly 0.1-0.2 mGy, so 150 µGy is a reasonable typical value.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The effective dose to a patient from a lung perfusion scan with 100 MBq Tc-99m is 1 mSv
stems.explanation: Tc-99m MAA delivers about 0.01 mSv per MBq, so 100 MBq gives an effective dose of approximately 1 mSv.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The average annual effective dose to the UK population from medical exposures is 400 µSv
stems.explanation: Medical exposures contribute roughly 0.4 mSv per person per year on average in the UK, about 15% of the total average annual dose of 2.7 mSv.

keyPoint: Benchmark values: barium enema ~7 mSv, chest X-ray ESD ~0.15 mGy, lung perfusion scan ~1 mSv, UK average medical dose ~0.4 mSv/year, public dose limit 1 mSv/year.

title: Concerning diagnostic ultrasound

stems.label: A
stems.text: A thicker transducer will emit ultrasound with a longer wavelength
stems.explanation: The crystal resonates at the frequency whose half-wavelength equals its thickness, so a thicker element produces a lower frequency and longer wavelength.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Amplitude and direction of blood flow can be assessed using power doppler
stems.explanation: Conventional power Doppler displays the total power (amplitude) of the Doppler signal but discards directional and velocity information.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The fastest flow that can be accurately measured is the velocity that produces a doppler shift frequency of half the PRF
stems.explanation: The Nyquist limit means Doppler shifts above half the pulse repetition frequency alias, so PRF/2 sets the maximum measurable shift.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Aliasing can be reduced by increasing the angle of insonation
stems.explanation: A larger beam-to-vessel angle reduces the detected Doppler shift (cosine dependence), bringing it back below the Nyquist limit, though velocity estimates become less accurate near 90 degrees.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Harmonic imaging improves lateral resolution
stems.explanation: Harmonics are generated preferentially in the strong central portion of the beam, giving a narrower effective beam with better lateral resolution and fewer artefacts.

keyPoint: Transducer thickness sets frequency, the Nyquist limit (PRF/2) caps measurable Doppler shift, and power Doppler trades directional information for sensitivity.

title: Under IRR (2017) an employee must become a classified worker if

stems.label: A
stems.text: The dose to their eyes is likely to exceed 20 mSv annually
stems.explanation: Classification is required if the lens dose is likely to exceed 15 mSv per year, so a worker likely to exceed 20 mSv (the annual eye dose limit) must certainly be classified.

stems.label: B
stems.text: They are likely to receive an annual effective dose greater than 6 mSv
stems.explanation: IRR 2017 requires classification when the effective dose is likely to exceed 6 mSv per year (three-tenths of the 20 mSv limit).

stems.label: C
stems.text: Four-tenths of a relevant dose limit is likely to be exceeded
stems.explanation: The classification threshold is three-tenths of a relevant equivalent dose limit, so anyone likely to exceed four-tenths has passed the threshold and must be classified.

stems.label: D
stems.text: They work in different locations
stems.explanation: Working at multiple sites relates to arrangements for outside workers and dose record keeping, not to whether classification is required.

stems.label: E
stems.text: They become pregnant
stems.explanation: Pregnancy triggers a risk assessment and dose restriction to the fetus (1 mSv for the remainder of the pregnancy), not classification.

keyPoint: Classification under IRR 2017 is triggered by likely doses above 6 mSv effective, 15 mSv to the eye lens, or three-tenths of any other relevant dose limit.

title: About CR systems

stems.label: A
stems.text: CR systems have a very wide dynamic range
stems.explanation: Photostimulable phosphor plates respond linearly over about four orders of magnitude of exposure, far wider than film.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Imaging plates are scanned with a blue laser to release stored energy from the X-ray exposure
stems.explanation: The plate is scanned with a red laser; the stimulated emission released from the storage phosphor is blue light collected by the photomultiplier.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Resolution is independent of pixel size
stems.explanation: Spatial resolution in CR is limited by the sampling pixel size (and laser spot/light spread), so smaller pixels give higher limiting resolution.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Any latent image is removed by exposure to high intensity white light
stems.explanation: After readout the plate is flooded with intense white light to empty remaining trapped electrons and erase any residual latent image.

stems.label: E
stems.text: CR gives lower radiation doses than DR radiography
stems.explanation: DR detectors have higher detective quantum efficiency than CR plates, so DR can achieve the same image quality at lower dose.

keyPoint: CR plates are read with a red laser, emit blue light, are erased with white light, and have wide dynamic range but lower dose efficiency than DR.

title: Regarding CT

stems.label: A
stems.text: It may be considered low dose radiological equipment
stems.explanation: CT is a high-dose modality, contributing the majority of medical radiation dose to the population despite being a minority of examinations.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Typical spatial resolution is in the region of 10 lp/cm
stems.explanation: CT spatial resolution is typically around 0.5-1 lp/mm, i.e. of the order of 5-10 lp/cm, much lower than plain radiography.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A CT image is usually reconstructed onto a 256x256 matrix
stems.explanation: The standard CT reconstruction matrix is 512x512.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The window width is the range of Hounsfield units covered by a structure
stems.explanation: Window width is the range of Hounsfield units mapped across the displayed grey scale, chosen by the operator, not a property of any structure.

stems.label: E
stems.text: A narrow window is used when variations in density are small
stems.explanation: A narrow window spreads a small HU range over the full grey scale, maximising displayed contrast between tissues of similar density.

keyPoint: CT is high-dose, reconstructs onto a 512 matrix with ~10 lp/cm resolution, and narrow display windows are used to show subtle density differences.

title: Principles of MRI

stems.label: A
stems.text: All MR active nuclei should have the same gyromagnetic ratio
stems.explanation: The gyromagnetic ratio is a characteristic constant of each nucleus; different MR-active nuclei (e.g. 1H, 31P, 23Na) have different ratios.

stems.label: B
stems.text: If the B0 is increased the Larmor frequency decreases
stems.explanation: The Larmor frequency is directly proportional to B0 (omega = gamma B0), so it increases with field strength.

stems.label: C
stems.text: In the body hydrogen produces signal essentially in just two molecules - water and fat
stems.explanation: Clinically useful MR signal comes almost entirely from mobile hydrogen nuclei in water and fat; protons in solids and macromolecules dephase too quickly.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Hydrogen in water precesses faster than in fat
stems.explanation: Water protons are less shielded than fat protons and precess at a slightly higher frequency, the basis of chemical shift.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The chemical shift between water and fat is expressed as 3.5 ppm
stems.explanation: The water-fat resonance difference is about 3.5 ppm, roughly 220 Hz at 1.5 T.

keyPoint: Larmor frequency is proportional to B0 via the nucleus-specific gyromagnetic ratio, and clinical signal comes from water and fat protons separated by 3.5 ppm.

title: Skin doses for interventional radiology patients may be reduced by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increasing the X-ray tube to intensifier distance
stems.explanation: Lengthening the tube-detector distance alone forces the automatic dose-rate control to raise tube output, tending to increase skin dose.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the X-ray tube to patient distance
stems.explanation: Moving the tube further from the patient reduces entrance skin dose by the inverse square law for the same detector dose rate.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increasing the patient to image intensifier distance
stems.explanation: An air gap between patient and detector increases magnification and makes the automatic exposure control drive up the dose rate, raising skin dose.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Angling the X-ray beam to the patient
stems.explanation: Steeply angled (oblique) projections lengthen the tissue path, so the dose-rate control increases output and skin dose rises.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Using a number of different projections
stems.explanation: Changing projection during long procedures spreads the entrance dose over different areas of skin, reducing the peak skin dose at any one site.

keyPoint: Keep the tube far from the patient, the detector close, avoid steep obliques, and vary the projection to spread entrance skin dose.

title: Regarding annual dose levels, dose limits and dose constraints

stems.label: A
stems.text: The annual effective dose from natural background radiation in the UK is approximately 2.7 mSv
stems.explanation: The average UK annual dose from all sources is about 2.7 mSv, most of it from natural background (radon, cosmic, terrestrial, internal).

stems.label: B
stems.text: The whole body dose limit for a member of the public is 6 mSv
stems.explanation: The annual effective dose limit for the public is 1 mSv; 6 mSv is the classification threshold for workers.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The annual whole body dose limit for a classified radiation worker is 20 mSv
stems.explanation: IRR 2017 sets the employee effective dose limit at 20 mSv per year.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The annual dose limit for exposure of an area of skin of a classified radiation worker is 500 mSv
stems.explanation: The equivalent dose limit for the skin of an employee is 500 mSv per year averaged over any 1 cm2.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The annual whole body dose which a non-classified radiation worker should not exceed is 1 mSv
stems.explanation: Non-classified workers may receive up to 6 mSv per year before classification is required; 1 mSv is the limit for members of the public.

keyPoint: Key figures: UK background ~2.7 mSv, worker limit 20 mSv, skin limit 500 mSv, public limit 1 mSv, and 6 mSv is the worker classification threshold.

title: The photoelectric effect

stems.label: A
stems.text: Represents the interaction between a photon and valence electron
stems.explanation: Photoelectric absorption involves an inner-shell (usually K-shell) electron whose binding energy is just below the photon energy; interactions with loosely bound valence electrons are Compton events.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Causes the atom to be ionized
stems.explanation: Ejection of the photoelectron leaves the atom ionised with an inner-shell vacancy.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Results in total absorption of the photon
stems.explanation: The incident photon disappears completely, its energy going to the photoelectron's binding and kinetic energy.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increases with photon energy
stems.explanation: The photoelectric probability falls steeply with energy, approximately as 1/E^3 (apart from step increases at absorption edges).

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is linear to the atomic number
stems.explanation: Photoelectric probability varies approximately with the cube of atomic number (Z^3), not linearly.

keyPoint: Photoelectric absorption completely absorbs the photon at an inner-shell electron, varying roughly as Z^3/E^3.

title: In computed tomography

stems.label: A
stems.text: Iterative reconstruction is commonly used in modern scanners
stems.explanation: Iterative reconstruction has largely supplemented or replaced pure filtered back projection on modern scanners, allowing noise and dose reduction.

stems.label: B
stems.text: A window level of 20 is useful for bone imaging
stems.explanation: A level of about 20-40 HU suits soft tissue; bone windows use a high level (several hundred HU) with a wide width.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The Hounsfield number of fat is about -100
stems.explanation: Fat typically measures around -80 to -120 HU, so -100 is a good representative value.

stems.label: D
stems.text: A pixel in an image is a representation of the average linear attenuation coefficient of a voxel
stems.explanation: Each displayed pixel encodes the mean linear attenuation coefficient of the corresponding tissue voxel, expressed relative to water in Hounsfield units.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The CT number of a voxel is determined only by the physical density of its contents
stems.explanation: Attenuation depends on both electron/physical density and effective atomic number (via Compton and photoelectric contributions), not density alone.

keyPoint: CT numbers encode average voxel attenuation relative to water (fat ~-100 HU) and depend on composition as well as density; iterative reconstruction is now standard.

title: Regarding the use of contrast media

stems.label: A
stems.text: Radio-opaque contrast media are chosen because they have a sufficiently high atomic number to maximise the absorption of diagnostic X-rays by the Compton effect
stems.explanation: High atomic number enhances photoelectric absorption (proportional to Z^3); Compton interactions are essentially independent of atomic number.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The absorption energy/K-edge of iodine is 53 keV
stems.explanation: The K-edge of iodine is 33.2 keV; 53 is iodine's atomic number, not its K-edge energy.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Bone and iodine demonstrate a similar computed tomography (CT) number because they have a similar atomic number
stems.explanation: Iodine (Z=53) has a much higher atomic number than calcium (Z=20); any similarity in CT numbers reflects concentration and density effects, not similar atomic number.

stems.label: D
stems.text: High density and low density contrast media can be administered together in certain circumstances to improve image contrast and quality
stems.explanation: Double-contrast techniques combine barium with gas (e.g. air or CO2) to coat mucosa and distend the lumen, improving contrast and detail.

stems.label: E
stems.text: A positive contrast agent should ideally have K-edge energy equal to the characteristic radiation emitted from the X-ray tube
stems.explanation: The ideal K-edge lies just below the mean energy of the beam spectrum to maximise photoelectric absorption, not matched to the tube's characteristic lines.

keyPoint: Contrast agents work through photoelectric absorption: iodine's K-edge at 33.2 keV sits just below typical mean beam energies, and double-contrast studies combine positive and negative agents.

title: Imaging geometry

stems.label: A
stems.text: Distortion is greater with a larger focus-detector distance
stems.explanation: A longer focus-detector distance reduces magnification and differential magnification, so distortion is less, not greater.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Geometrical unsharpness occurs only with round-edged objects
stems.explanation: Penumbra arises from the finite focal spot size and affects the edges of all objects regardless of shape.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Object-detector distance is directly related to unsharpness
stems.explanation: Increasing the object-detector distance increases magnification and hence the penumbra, worsening geometric unsharpness.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Magnification in mammography is achieved by increasing object-detector distance
stems.explanation: Magnification views raise the breast on a platform away from the detector, using a fine focal spot and air gap to magnify with acceptable sharpness.

stems.label: E
stems.text: An ideal set-up would minimise focal spot size, maximise focus-detector distance and minimise object-detector distance
stems.explanation: Small focus, long FDD and short ODD together minimise magnification and penumbra, giving the sharpest image.

keyPoint: Sharpness is optimised with a small focal spot, long focus-detector distance and short object-detector distance; deliberately increasing ODD produces magnification.

title: Concerning biological effects of ionising radiation

stems.label: A
stems.text: Most damage to cells occurs as a result of a direct "hit" from a photon
stems.explanation: For low-LET radiation about two-thirds of DNA damage is indirect, mediated by free radicals from water radiolysis.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Linear energy transfer (LET) is defined as the energy deposited in tissue per unit path length
stems.explanation: LET is the energy transferred to the medium per unit track length, typically quoted in keV per micrometre.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Radiation with a high LET is more damaging to biological tissues
stems.explanation: Densely ionising high-LET radiation produces clustered, less repairable DNA damage, so its relative biological effectiveness is greater.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Alpha particles have a much lower LET than beta particles
stems.explanation: Alpha particles are heavy and doubly charged, giving a far higher LET than beta particles.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Relative biological effectiveness (RBE) is the ratio of absorbed doses required to induce the same biological endpoint for two different radiation types
stems.explanation: RBE compares the dose of a reference radiation with the dose of the test radiation needed to produce the same biological effect.

keyPoint: Most low-LET damage is indirect via free radicals; high-LET particles like alpha are far more biologically damaging per unit dose (higher RBE).

title: Justification and optimisation

stems.label: A
stems.text: Only radiologists and radiographers are allowed to take the role of the practitioner under Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposures) Regs (IR(ME)R) 2017
stems.explanation: Any registered healthcare professional entitled under the employer's procedures (e.g. dentists, cardiologists, nuclear medicine physicians) may act as practitioner.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It is possible for one person to be the referrer, practitioner and operator for an examination
stems.explanation: One suitably entitled individual (for example a dentist) may legitimately hold all three duty-holder roles for a single exposure.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Optimisation is the process of obtaining the best quality image possible
stems.explanation: Optimisation means keeping doses as low as reasonably practicable while achieving image quality adequate for the clinical purpose, not maximal quality.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The referrer is not responsible for justifying the radiation dose to the patient
stems.explanation: Justification is the practitioner's responsibility; the referrer must supply sufficient clinical information to enable it.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The practitioner has overall responsibility for compliance with IR(ME)R
stems.explanation: Overall responsibility for the IR(ME)R framework rests with the employer; the practitioner is responsible for justification of individual exposures.

keyPoint: Under IR(ME)R the employer holds overall responsibility, the practitioner justifies, the referrer supplies clinical information, and one person may hold multiple roles.

title: Gamma photons

stems.label: A
stems.text: Are released from a rotating anode overcouch system when a high voltage current is passed across the tube
stems.explanation: X-ray tubes produce X-rays from electron interactions at the anode; gamma photons originate from transitions within an unstable nucleus.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Can be considered as both a particle and a wave
stems.explanation: Like all electromagnetic radiation, gamma photons show wave-particle duality.

stems.label: C
stems.text: If sufficiently energetic can remove electrons from their orbiting shell around a nucleus
stems.explanation: Gamma photons are ionising radiation and can eject bound electrons by photoelectric or Compton interactions.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Can be emitted by an atom without changing its atomic mass or number
stems.explanation: Gamma emission (e.g. isomeric transition of Tc-99m) de-excites the nucleus without changing Z or A.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Are more penetrative than alpha and beta radiation
stems.explanation: Uncharged gamma photons interact much less readily than charged alpha or beta particles and therefore penetrate much further in matter.

keyPoint: Gamma rays are nuclear in origin, leave atomic number and mass unchanged, and being uncharged are far more penetrating than alpha or beta particles.

title: The following are true of electromagnetic radiation

stems.label: A
stems.text: It travels in straight lines unless attenuated
stems.explanation: Photons travel in straight lines until they interact; scatter interactions during attenuation can deflect them from the original path.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The intensity of radiation emitted from a point source will reduce in inverse proportion to the square of the distance from that point source
stems.explanation: The inverse square law follows from the geometric divergence of radiation from a point source.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The frequency of electromagnetic radiation is inversely proportional to its wavelength
stems.explanation: Since c = f x lambda and c is constant, frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Doubling the distance from a point source will reduce the radiation intensity by 50%
stems.explanation: Doubling distance reduces intensity to one quarter (a 75% reduction) by the inverse square law.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The inverse square law will predict the reduction in intensity of a beam of radiation from a point source passing through lead
stems.explanation: Attenuation in a medium is exponential and governed by the attenuation coefficient; the inverse square law only describes geometric divergence in the absence of attenuation.

keyPoint: The inverse square law describes divergence only — doubling distance quarters intensity — while transmission through matter follows exponential attenuation.

title: Radiation protection

stems.label: A
stems.text: The main source of radiation to staff is due to scatter from the patient
stems.explanation: Staff dose in radiology comes predominantly from Compton scatter off the patient, not from the primary beam or tube leakage.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The risk of developing fatal childhood cancer from radiation exposure in utero is around 1 in 13,000 per mGy
stems.explanation: The commonly quoted excess risk of childhood cancer after in utero exposure is approximately 1 in 13,000 per mGy of fetal dose.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Thermoluminescent detectors can directly measure entrance surface dose
stems.explanation: TLD chips placed on the skin measure entrance surface dose directly, including backscatter.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Deterministic effects are best measured by DAP
stems.explanation: Deterministic skin effects depend on peak local skin dose; dose-area product spreads dose over the whole field and correlates poorly with peak skin dose.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Entrance surface dose is proportional to kV2
stems.explanation: Tube output, and hence entrance surface dose at fixed mAs and geometry, rises approximately with the square of the applied kV.

keyPoint: Staff dose is dominated by patient scatter; peak skin dose (not DAP) predicts deterministic effects, and TLDs measure entrance surface dose directly.

title: In MRI

stems.label: A
stems.text: Flowing blood appear dark on GRE
stems.explanation: On gradient echo sequences inflowing blood is typically bright due to flow-related enhancement, the basis of time-of-flight angiography.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Venous blood appear as 'flow voids' on spin echo sequences
stems.explanation: Flow voids on spin echo occur with fast (arterial) flow; slow venous flow often returns relatively high signal through flow-related enhancement.

stems.label: C
stems.text: In PD weighted sequences, a short TE reduces the effect of T2
stems.explanation: Proton density weighting uses long TR (minimising T1 effects) and short TE so that little T2 decay occurs before readout.

stems.label: D
stems.text: 'Ghost' artefacts appear in the phase encoding direction
stems.explanation: Periodic motion (pulsation, respiration) produces ghost replicas displaced along the phase-encoding axis because phase encoding is built up over many TRs.

stems.label: E
stems.text: 'Ringing' artefact can be reduced by reducing the matrix
stems.explanation: Gibbs (truncation) ringing is worse with coarser sampling; increasing the matrix (more phase-encode steps) reduces it.

keyPoint: Fast flow gives spin echo flow voids while GRE shows flowing blood bright; ghosts propagate in the phase-encode direction and Gibbs ringing is reduced by a larger matrix.

title: Concerning radiation dose in mammography

stems.label: A
stems.text: The radiation dose is quoted in terms of the effective dose
stems.explanation: Mammography dose is quoted as the mean glandular dose, since glandular tissue is the tissue at risk.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The radiation dose is measured in mGy
stems.explanation: Mean glandular dose is an absorbed dose and is expressed in milligray.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The national dose reference level in the UK is 5 mGy
stems.explanation: UK reference values for mean glandular dose per view for a standard breast are well below 5 mGy; the NHSBSP standard is less than 2.5 mGy per view.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The dose must be <2.5 mGy per image for a standard breast in the UK NHS breast screening programme
stems.explanation: The NHSBSP requires the mean glandular dose to a standard breast to be under 2.5 mGy per view.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The glandular tissue in the breast is the most sensitive to radiation
stems.explanation: Glandular epithelium is the radiosensitive tissue at risk of carcinogenesis, which is why dose is expressed as mean glandular dose.

keyPoint: Mammography dose is expressed as mean glandular dose in mGy, kept below 2.5 mGy per view for a standard breast in the NHSBSP.

title: With regards to inversion recovery pulse sequence

stems.label: A
stems.text: Begins with a 90 degree pulse
stems.explanation: Inversion recovery begins with a 180 degree inverting pulse, followed after the inversion time TI by a 90 degree excitation pulse.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Excellent T2 contrast
stems.explanation: Classical inversion recovery gives heavily T1-weighted contrast; the inversion pulse manipulates longitudinal magnetisation.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Has a relatively short TR
stems.explanation: IR sequences need a long TR to allow full longitudinal recovery between inversions, making them relatively slow.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Short tau inversion recovery is a good fat suppressing technique
stems.explanation: STIR uses a short TI (~150-170 ms at 1.5 T) timed to the null point of fat, suppressing fat signal.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) has a long tau (TI)
stems.explanation: FLAIR uses a long TI (~2000 ms) to null the signal from CSF.

keyPoint: Inversion recovery starts with a 180 degree pulse and long TR; a short TI nulls fat (STIR) and a long TI nulls CSF (FLAIR).

title: Regarding positron emission tomography (PET)

stems.label: A
stems.text: PET involves the detection of gamma photons with energies in the range 100-200 keV
stems.explanation: PET detects pairs of 511 keV annihilation photons, well above the 100-200 keV range of single-photon imaging.

stems.label: B
stems.text: PET utilizes positron-emitting radionuclides with long half-lives
stems.explanation: PET tracers such as F-18 (110 min), C-11 (20 min) and O-15 (2 min) have short half-lives, which is why many require an on-site or nearby cyclotron.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Coincidence detection eliminates the need for lead collimators
stems.explanation: Electronic coincidence detection of the two back-to-back photons localises events without physical collimation, giving PET much higher sensitivity than SPECT.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Single pair of detectors rotate around the patient
stems.explanation: Modern PET scanners use complete stationary rings of detectors surrounding the patient.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is a low dose technique
stems.explanation: A typical FDG PET study gives an effective dose of several mSv, and combined PET-CT doses are higher still; it is not a low-dose technique.

keyPoint: PET detects coincident 511 keV annihilation photons with detector rings and no collimators, using short-lived cyclotron-produced positron emitters.

title: In the production of X-rays

stems.label: A
stems.text: Bremsstrahlung refers to the energy gained by electrons as they are accelerated towards the target
stems.explanation: Bremsstrahlung ('braking radiation') is emitted when electrons decelerate and deflect in the field of target nuclei, not while gaining energy across the tube.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Thermionic emission occurs in the target
stems.explanation: Thermionic emission of electrons occurs at the heated filament of the cathode, not at the target.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Bremsstrahlung radiation is formed at the cathode of an X-ray tube
stems.explanation: Bremsstrahlung is produced at the anode target where the accelerated electrons are stopped.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Characteristic radiation is formed at the anode of an X-ray tube
stems.explanation: Characteristic X-rays are emitted at the anode when inner-shell vacancies created by bombarding electrons are refilled.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Only about 50% of the energy of the bombarding electrons is emitted as useful x-ray radiation
stems.explanation: Only about 1% of the electron energy becomes X-rays at diagnostic tube voltages; some 99% is deposited as heat in the anode.

keyPoint: Electrons are emitted thermionically at the cathode and produce bremsstrahlung and characteristic X-rays at the anode, with only ~1% efficiency.

title: Concerning diagnostic reference levels (DRLs)

stems.label: A
stems.text: DRLs for selected radiological examinations are set nationally
stems.explanation: National DRLs are published for common examinations from national dose survey data; employers also set local DRLs informed by them.

stems.label: B
stems.text: If a patient receives a dose greater than the DRL, the employer must report this to the IRMER inspectorate
stems.explanation: DRLs are not dose limits; consistently exceeding them triggers local investigation and corrective action, not statutory reporting of individual patients.

stems.label: C
stems.text: DRL in radionuclide imaging is expressed in activity administered
stems.explanation: For nuclear medicine, DRLs are set as administered activity in MBq for each procedure.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The employer must audit local DRLs
stems.explanation: IR(ME)R requires employers to establish local DRLs and regularly review/audit doses against them.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Aging equipment is a justified reason to exceed DRLs
stems.explanation: DRLs should be achievable with standard equipment and good technique; old equipment performance is a reason for investigation and replacement, not justification.

keyPoint: DRLs are audit tools, not limits: set nationally and locally, expressed as administered activity in nuclear medicine, and consistent excess demands investigation.

title: Scatter and grids

stems.label: A
stems.text: Scatter predominantly affects spatial resolution
stems.explanation: Scatter adds a relatively uniform background that degrades image contrast; its effect on spatial resolution is minimal.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the kV reduces the scatter reaching the plate or detector
stems.explanation: Higher kV produces more forward-directed, more penetrating scatter, so the scatter fraction reaching the detector increases.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Grid techniques reduce scatter reaching the plate or detector
stems.explanation: Grid septa absorb obliquely travelling scattered photons while transmitting most of the primary beam.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Grid techniques increase image contrast resolution
stems.explanation: By removing scatter, grids restore subject contrast and improve the visibility of low-contrast detail.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Grid techniques reduce patient dose
stems.explanation: Grids absorb some primary radiation, so exposure must be increased by the Bucky factor (typically 3-5x), increasing patient dose.

keyPoint: Scatter degrades contrast rather than resolution; grids restore contrast at the cost of increased patient dose (Bucky factor).

title: Noise in CT

stems.label: A
stems.text: Noise limits CT as it reduces contrast and limits the resolution of small low contrast objects
stems.explanation: Quantum mottle determines low-contrast detectability, which is the main practical limit of CT image quality.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Quantum noise is the most significant type of noise in CT
stems.explanation: Statistical fluctuation in the number of detected photons (quantum noise) dominates over electronic and reconstruction noise in normal operation.

stems.label: C
stems.text: SNR may be increased by increasing the mA or scan time per rotation
stems.explanation: More mAs means more detected photons per voxel, reducing relative quantum noise and improving SNR (at increased dose).

stems.label: D
stems.text: SNR may be increased by reducing the slice width on multi-slice scanners
stems.explanation: Thinner slices collect fewer photons per voxel, so noise increases and SNR falls.

stems.label: E
stems.text: If the mA is kept constant increasing the kV will increase the SNR
stems.explanation: Higher kV increases both tube output and beam penetration, so more photons reach the detectors and quantum noise falls.

keyPoint: Quantum noise governs CT low-contrast performance; SNR improves with more mAs, higher kV or thicker slices, all trading against dose or resolution.

title: Concerning ultrasound transducers

stems.label: A
stems.text: In a linear array transducer, electronic focusing is achieved by triggering inner elements before the outer ones
stems.explanation: Electronic focusing fires the outer elements first and the central elements last, so the wavelets converge at the focal depth.

stems.label: B
stems.text: A curvilinear array produces a sector shaped field
stems.explanation: The convex element arrangement produces a diverging, sector-shaped field of view that widens with depth.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Reducing the sector width increases the frame rate of a phased array
stems.explanation: A narrower sector needs fewer scan lines per frame, so frames can be acquired faster.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Beam steering is optimal with an annular array
stems.explanation: Annular arrays can focus electronically but cannot steer the beam electronically; steering requires mechanical movement.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Require a thin matching layer as well as the coupling agent
stems.explanation: A quarter-wavelength matching layer on the transducer face, plus coupling gel on the skin, minimises impedance mismatch and maximises energy transfer.

keyPoint: Array focusing relies on firing outer elements first, matching layers and gel manage impedance steps, and annular arrays cannot steer electronically.

title: Collimation and filtration in CT

stems.label: A
stems.text: Filtration in CT is typically 2.5mm aluminium equivalent
stems.explanation: CT beams are much more heavily filtered than the 2.5 mm Al minimum for radiography, using several mm of aluminium plus shaped (bow-tie) filters.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Bow tie filters are used to minimise variance in beam hardening caused by the elliptical shape of the patient
stems.explanation: The bow-tie filter compensates for the thinner peripheral path through the patient, equalising beam hardening and detector signal across the fan.

stems.label: C
stems.text: To produce 0.5mm images in multi-slice CT the collimation is set to a single row of detectors within the array
stems.explanation: Multi-slice CT opens the collimation to cover many detector rows simultaneously; thin images come from the individual row width, not single-row collimation.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Post-patient collimation is essential in multi-slice CT to prevent scatter
stems.explanation: Z-axis post-patient collimation is not possible with wide multi-row detectors; scatter is controlled with inter-detector septa instead.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The width of the collimation at the isocentre is typically about 50cm
stems.explanation: Beam collimation at the isocentre is millimetres to a few centimetres in the z-direction; about 50 cm describes the scan field of view, not the collimation.

keyPoint: CT uses heavy filtration with bow-tie filters to flatten the beam profile, and multi-slice scanners collimate the beam over many detector rows a few centimetres wide.

title: In digital subtraction angiography the input dose rate to the patient

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is reduced by using 0.2 mm copper
stems.explanation: Copper filtration removes low-energy photons that would be absorbed in the skin, reducing the input (entrance) dose rate.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is increased as the preferred method to improve image quality
stems.explanation: Increasing dose rate is a last resort; image quality should first be optimised through filtration, collimation, geometry and processing.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Can be monitored using a dose area product meter
stems.explanation: A DAP meter mounted on the tube assembly continuously monitors the radiation delivered during the procedure.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Must be increased with decreasing field size to maintain image quality
stems.explanation: Electronic magnification with a smaller input field requires a higher input dose rate to keep the same noise level in the displayed image.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is reduced when faster frame rates are used
stems.explanation: Higher frame rates mean more exposures per second, so the total dose rate to the patient increases.

keyPoint: Copper filtration lowers DSA entrance dose rate, magnification and higher frame rates raise it, and DAP meters monitor delivered dose.

title: Regarding the pulse echo principle

stems.label: A
stems.text: More information about the location and size of the reflector can be obtained if the beam is narrow
stems.explanation: A narrow beam improves lateral resolution, localising reflectors more accurately in the scan plane.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The speed of sound in most soft tissues is similar
stems.explanation: Soft tissue sound speeds cluster around 1540 m/s, the assumed average used by scanners for depth calculation.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The strength of the echoes decreases with depth
stems.explanation: Attenuation (mainly absorption) weakens both the transmitted pulse and returning echoes with increasing depth, which is why TGC is needed.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Time corrected gain (TGC) can be manually altered
stems.explanation: TGC applies operator-adjustable amplification that increases with echo arrival time to compensate for depth-dependent attenuation.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Ultrasound is not emitted continuously from the transducer
stems.explanation: B-mode imaging uses short pulses with listening intervals between them; the pulse-echo timing provides depth information.

keyPoint: Pulse-echo imaging assumes ~1540 m/s in soft tissue, uses short pulses with TGC to compensate for depth attenuation, and localises best with a narrow beam.

title: Spin echo pulse sequence

stems.label: A
stems.text: Begins with a 90 degree RF pulse followed by two 90 degree RF pulses
stems.explanation: Spin echo begins with a 90 degree excitation pulse followed by one (or more) 180 degree refocusing pulses, not further 90 degree pulses.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The purpose of the 90 degree pulse is to produce a transverse magnetization
stems.explanation: The 90 degree pulse tips longitudinal magnetisation into the transverse plane where it can induce signal in the receiver coil.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The purpose of the 180 degree pulse is to flip the magnetization through the transverse plane and refocus the spins
stems.explanation: The 180 degree pulse reverses the accumulated phase of dephasing spins so they refocus into an echo, cancelling fixed field inhomogeneity effects.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The time between the 90 degree pulse and the formation of the echo is known as TR is under the operators control
stems.explanation: The 90-degree-pulse-to-echo interval is the echo time TE; TR is the repetition time between successive 90 degree pulses.

stems.label: E
stems.text: If the operator selects 20msec for TE, the 180 degree pulse will be applied 20msec after the 90 degree pulse
stems.explanation: The 180 degree pulse is applied at TE/2, so for TE of 20 ms it occurs 10 ms after the 90 degree pulse.

keyPoint: Spin echo = 90 degree excitation then a 180 degree refocusing pulse at TE/2, producing an echo at TE; TR is the interval between excitations.

title: Nuclear Medicine

stems.label: A
stems.text: Technetium-99m has a gamma energy of 150keV
stems.explanation: Tc-99m emits gamma photons at 140 keV.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Fluorine-18 is produced in a generator with a half life of 110 minutes
stems.explanation: F-18 does have a 110 minute half-life, but it is produced in a cyclotron, not a generator.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Detectors in gamma cameras are made from bismuth germanate
stems.explanation: Gamma cameras use sodium iodide (thallium-activated) crystals; bismuth germanate is a PET detector material.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Collimators with wider holes reduce patient dose
stems.explanation: Patient dose is set by the administered activity, not the collimator; wider holes increase sensitivity at the expense of resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Thicker septa increase sensitivity at higher gamma energies
stems.explanation: Thicker septa are needed at higher energies to prevent septal penetration, but they reduce sensitivity by blocking more photons.

keyPoint: Tc-99m emits at 140 keV, F-18 is cyclotron-produced, gamma cameras use NaI(Tl), and collimator design trades sensitivity against resolution without changing patient dose.

title: The effective dose to a patient from a single radiograph under automatic exposure control

stems.label: A
stems.text: Decreased at lower mA
stems.explanation: Under AEC a lower mA simply lengthens the exposure time until the same detector dose is reached, so patient dose is essentially unchanged.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Decreased by the use of grids
stems.explanation: Grids absorb part of the beam, so the AEC increases exposure by the Bucky factor and patient dose rises.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Decreased by using a faster detector
stems.explanation: A more sensitive (faster) detector system needs less air kerma to reach the AEC cut-off, lowering patient dose.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Decreased by decreasing the field size
stems.explanation: Tighter collimation irradiates less tissue volume, reducing the effective dose even though the AEC may slightly increase exposure to compensate for lost scatter.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Always less than 5 mSv
stems.explanation: Even the highest-dose plain radiographs (lumbar spine, abdomen, pelvis) give effective doses of roughly 0.5-1.5 mSv, well below 5 mSv.

keyPoint: With AEC, patient dose is governed by detector sensitivity, grids and collimation rather than mA selection, and single radiographs stay well under 5 mSv.

title: In a normal radiographic set up

stems.label: A
stems.text: A shorter focus-receptor distance reduces the magnification
stems.explanation: Shortening the focus-receptor distance increases magnification; a long FRD is used to minimise it.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The smaller the object the greater the magnification
stems.explanation: Magnification is determined by the ratio of focus-receptor to focus-object distances and is independent of the object's size.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The image of an object increases in size as its distance from the image receptor increases
stems.explanation: Moving the object away from the receptor (closer to the focus) increases geometric magnification.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The image of an object increases in sharpness as its distance from the image receptor decreases
stems.explanation: A smaller object-receptor distance reduces magnification and penumbra, improving sharpness.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The magnification depends on the focal spot size
stems.explanation: Focal spot size affects geometric unsharpness (penumbra) but not the degree of magnification, which depends only on the geometry of the distances.

keyPoint: Magnification depends only on the focus-object-receptor geometry; focal spot size controls unsharpness, not magnification.

title: With regard to the Ionising Radiation Medical Exposure Regulations

stems.label: A
stems.text: They do not apply to exposures incurred during health screening
stems.explanation: IRMER applies to diagnosis, therapy, health screening, occupational health surveillance, medico-legal exposures, research and any exposure of an asymptomatic individual.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Radiographers & nurses can act as a practitioner
stems.explanation: Any registered healthcare professional can act as a practitioner, provided they are appropriately trained and entitled by the employer.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Optimisation of an exposure means delivering a radiation dose sufficient to obtain the best image quality
stems.explanation: That would encourage high doses; optimisation means using a dose just sufficient to provide the relevant diagnostic information.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Justification of an exposure ensures the difference between risk and benefit of the procedure is maximized.
stems.explanation: Justification is the process of determining that a procedure will produce a net benefit; maximising the risk-benefit margin describes optimisation.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Individual duty holders can be prosecuted if they breach the regulations
stems.explanation: Any duty holder named in IRMER may be prosecuted individually for failing to meet their obligations under the regulations.

keyPoint: IRMER covers all medical exposures including screening; justification establishes net benefit, optimisation keeps the dose to the minimum needed for diagnosis, and named duty holders are individually liable.

title: The calculated CT number of a pixel in a transaxial CT slice is affected by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: The CT number reflects the tissue's attenuation relative to water, and attenuation properties change with x-ray energy, which the kVp determines.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Changing the mA does not change the energy of the x-rays, so tissue attenuation and hence CT number are unaffected.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Slice thickness
stems.explanation: Thicker slices produce more partial volume effects, since the CT number is an average across all tissues within the voxel.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Surrounding patient anatomy
stems.explanation: Beam hardening through dense bone raises the mean beam energy, making downstream tissues appear less attenuating so their CT numbers decrease.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Reconstruction algorithm used
stems.explanation: The reconstruction algorithm affects the resolution and noise properties of the slices, which in turn can alter the CT numbers.

keyPoint: CT numbers depend on x-ray energy (kVp), slice thickness (partial volume), surrounding anatomy (beam hardening) and the reconstruction algorithm - but not on tube current.

title: Increasing the pitch of a MDCT scan from 1.0 to 1.5 will have the following effects

stems.label: A
stems.text: Reduced image noise
stems.explanation: A higher pitch acquires fewer projections, so less data is used for reconstruction and image noise actually increases.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Reduced patient dose
stems.explanation: With pitch above 1 the table moves further than the beam width per rotation, so a smaller volume of tissue is irradiated and dose falls.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Reduced scan time
stems.explanation: A higher pitch moves the table faster, covering more anatomy in the same time and shortening the scan.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Reduced partial volume artifacts
stems.explanation: Z-plane resolution is degraded at higher pitch, resulting in greater averaging between gantry rotations.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Reduced patient motion artifacts
stems.explanation: A shorter scan gives less opportunity for patient motion during acquisition.

keyPoint: Raising pitch above 1 shortens the scan and lowers dose and motion artefact, at the cost of increased noise and degraded z-axis (partial volume) resolution.

title: Decreasing each of the following parameters will reduce the noise in a MDCT study

stems.label: A
stems.text: Gantry rotation speed
stems.explanation: A slower rotation means a longer acquisition time per rotation, so more x-rays are detected and statistical noise falls.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Slice thickness
stems.explanation: Thinner slices use fewer photons per voxel, which increases statistical (random) noise.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Tube votage (kVp)
stems.explanation: Lower kVp produces fewer x-ray photons at the detector, which increases noise.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Matrix size
stems.explanation: A smaller matrix (e.g. 512x512 down to 256x256) means larger pixels, so more x-rays are recorded per pixel and statistical noise is reduced.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Lower mA emits fewer photons per second so fewer are detected, increasing statistical noise.

keyPoint: CT noise falls when more photons contribute to each pixel - slower rotation or a smaller matrix helps, whereas reducing slice thickness, kVp or mA all increase noise.

title: In MR imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: The frequency of electromagnetic radiation needed to excite nuclei is proportional to the static magnetic field strength
stems.explanation: The resonant (Larmor) frequency of the nuclei is proportional to the magnetic field strength.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The direction of the static magnetic field must be parallel to the long axis of the body
stems.explanation: The main magnetic field can be applied in any direction.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A magnetic field gradient is used to define the slice to be imaged
stems.explanation: The gradient makes the Larmor frequency vary with position, so an RF pulse at one frequency excites only the slice whose Larmor frequency matches it.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Gadolinium-based contrast agents shorten both T1 and T2 of tissues
stems.explanation: Gadolinium is paramagnetic and shortens both T1 and T2, although the effect on T1 is much greater.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Hydrogen nuclei in fat and water precess at the same frequency
stems.explanation: Protons in fat and water precess at slightly different frequencies because of differing magnetic shielding by their orbital electrons (chemical shift).

keyPoint: The Larmor frequency is proportional to field strength and is exploited by gradients for slice selection; gadolinium shortens T1 (and T2), and fat and water protons precess at slightly different frequencies.

title: Compton scattering

stems.label: A
stems.text: Predominantly involves K-shell electrons
stems.explanation: Compton scattering occurs when the electron binding energy is much lower than the photon energy, so it usually involves weakly bound outer-shell electrons.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Occurs more frequently with increasing tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: The probability of Compton scattering decreases slowly with increasing photon energy (or kVp).

stems.label: C
stems.text: Degrades image contrast in x-ray and nuclear medicine studies
stems.explanation: Scattered x-rays (or gamma rays) are redirected from their original path and always degrade image contrast.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is the predominant mode of interaction in patients during CT procedures
stems.explanation: The average photon energy in CT beams is ~70 keV, making Compton scattering much more likely than the photoelectric effect in soft tissue.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is the predominant mode of interaction in the input screen of an image intensifier
stems.explanation: The input screen uses a CsI phosphor; its high atomic number favours photoelectric interactions rather than Compton scattering.

keyPoint: Compton scattering involves outer-shell electrons, dominates in soft tissue at diagnostic CT energies, and is the main source of contrast-degrading scatter.

title: Scattered radiation in abdominal radiography can be reduced by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increasing the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Increasing the mA increases both the incident x-rays and the scattered x-rays in the transmitted beam, so the scatter fraction remains constant.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Making the x-ray beam more collimated
stems.explanation: Increasing collimation reduces the x-ray field size, which reduces the volume of tissue that can generate scatter.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Compressing the abdomen
stems.explanation: Tissue compression, as also used in mammography, reduces the volume of tissue which can generate scatter.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Reducing the tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: Lower kVp promotes photoelectric interactions, and scatter that does occur is directed through larger angles (more backscatter) and so misses the image receptor.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the patient-to-image receptor distance
stems.explanation: An air gap lets scattered radiation diverge away from the image receptor and go undetected, though it produces a magnified image.

keyPoint: Scatter reaching the receptor is reduced by collimation, compression, lower kVp and an air gap — but not by changing mA, which scales primary and scatter alike.

title: The ideal properties of a radionuclide for imaging with a gamma camera include

stems.label: A
stems.text: A physical half-life less than or equal to 1 hour
stems.explanation: So short a half-life would limit shelf life and require constant replenishment; the ideal half-life is 4-6 hours.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Gamma ray emission in an energy range 0.1-0.2MeV
stems.explanation: Photons below this range are largely absorbed in the patient (higher dose), while those above it are harder to collimate and detect.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Does not decay via electron capture
stems.explanation: Electron capture can yield an excited daughter that emits a gamma ray; I-123 and In-111 both decay by electron capture and are used for imaging.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Decays to a non-radioactive daughter
stems.explanation: A radioactive daughter would further irradiate the patient and increase their radiation dose.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is cyclotron produced
stems.explanation: Cyclotron production is expensive and not always available; radionuclide generators provide a cheaper, readily available supply.

keyPoint: The ideal imaging radionuclide has a 4-6 hour half-life, 100-200 keV gamma emission, a stable daughter, and is generator-produced — electron capture decay is acceptable.

title: Regarding the gamma camera

stems.label: A
stems.text: The NaI crystal has a detection efficiency of about 90% for 140keV gamma rays
stems.explanation: NaI has a high atomic number and high density, giving high detection efficiency for 140 keV gamma rays.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The spatial resolution of the camera is largely controlled by the thickness of the NaI scintillation crystal
stems.explanation: The collimator has the largest influence on the spatial resolution of a gamma camera.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The detected count rate is proportional to the activity administered to the patient for activities up 1GBq
stems.explanation: Proportionality holds only at low activities; at higher activities dead-time effects mean the camera cannot accurately register all gamma rays reaching the detector.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Septal penetration may occur when imaging radionuclides which emit gamma rays with energy >200keV
stems.explanation: A small amount of septal penetration occurs in all studies, but it becomes more likely for higher-energy gamma rays.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Less than 0.1% of the gamma rays emitted from a patient are utilized to form an image
stems.explanation: Most emitted gamma rays are directed away from the camera, absorbed in the collimator, or rejected as scatter by the pulse height analyser window.

keyPoint: Gamma camera performance is collimator-limited: NaI detects 140 keV photons efficiently, but dead time, septal penetration and collimator losses mean under 0.1% of emissions form the image.

title: The radiation dose to a patient from injected radiopharmaceuticals

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases in direct proportion to the biological half-life
stems.explanation: A longer biological residence time does increase the dose, but the relationship is not one of direct proportionality.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Depends on the properties of both the radionuclide and the pharmaceutical
stems.explanation: The physical properties of the radionuclide (half-life, emissions) and the biochemical distribution and residence time of the pharmaceutical both affect the dose.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Is delivered at a much lower dose rate than in CT studies
stems.explanation: The dose from a radiopharmaceutical is delivered over several hours, whereas in CT the dose is delivered in a few seconds.

stems.label: D
stems.text: May be measured using a gamma camera
stems.explanation: The gamma camera can only measure activity distributions in the patient, not radiation dose.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is a factor which limits the quality of radionuclide images
stems.explanation: Low activities must be administered to minimise patient dose, but this results in noisy images.

keyPoint: Radiopharmaceutical dose depends on both radionuclide physics and pharmaceutical kinetics, is delivered slowly at low dose rate, cannot be measured by the gamma camera, and constrains image quality.

title: In clinical CT scanning

stems.label: A
stems.text: The transmitted x-ray intensity is measured by an array of scintillation detectors
stems.explanation: The detectors are scintillators, typically made of gadolinium oxysulphide.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The x-ray beam is heavily filtered using copper or tin filters
stems.explanation: The beam is pre-hardened using heavy filtration to remove low-energy bremsstrahlung x-rays.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The x-ray beam is pulsed during acquisition to reduce patient dose
stems.explanation: The x-ray tube is continuously energised as it rotates around the patient.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Focal spot sizes of 0.6mm and 1.2mm are typically used
stems.explanation: Fine and broad focal spot sizes of this order are available on CT tubes.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The pitch is the distance moved by the imaging table in a single rotation divided by the slice thickness
stems.explanation: Pitch is the distance moved by the table per rotation divided by the collimated beam width, not the slice thickness.

keyPoint: CT uses continuously energised tubes with heavily filtered beams, gadolinium oxysulphide scintillation detectors, dual focal spots, and pitch defined relative to collimated beam width.

title: An increase in operating frequency in ultrasound studies will result in the following

stems.label: A
stems.text: An improvement in axial resolution
stems.explanation: Increasing the operating frequency improves both axial and lateral resolution.

stems.label: B
stems.text: No change in the speed of US wave propagation
stems.explanation: Wave speed depends on the properties of the medium through which it travels, not on the frequency.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increased risk of thermal damage
stems.explanation: Absorption increases with frequency and results in greater tissue heating.

stems.label: D
stems.text: A reduced incidence of aliasing artifacts in Doppler scans
stems.explanation: The Doppler shift increases with operating frequency, so aliasing artefacts become more likely, not less.

stems.label: E
stems.text: An increase in signal strength from distal structures
stems.explanation: Echoes from deep structures are weaker at higher frequencies because attenuation increases with frequency.

keyPoint: Raising ultrasound frequency improves resolution and increases heating and Doppler aliasing, while leaving propagation speed unchanged and weakening echoes from depth.

title: Regarding x-ray production

stems.label: A
stems.text: Bremsstrahlung x-rays are emitted when an electron interacts with the nucleus of an atom in the target
stems.explanation: The electron undergoes a sudden deceleration in the field of the nucleus and the change in kinetic energy is released as an x-ray photon.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The efficiency of bremsstrahlung emission is typically 10% in diagnostic x-ray tubes
stems.explanation: In diagnostic radiology only about 1% of the electron energy striking the target is emitted as bremsstrahlung x-rays.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Bremsstrahlung production is more efficient at higher tube voltages
stems.explanation: The probability of bremsstrahlung interactions is proportional to the atomic number of the target multiplied by the tube voltage, so more bremsstrahlung x-rays are emitted at higher kVp.

stems.label: D
stems.text: For a tungsten x-ray target both L-shell and K-shell characteristic x-rays can reach the image receptor
stems.explanation: Characteristic x-rays from the L-shell are of very low energy and are easily absorbed in the patient before reaching the receptor.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The energy of K-shell characteristic x-rays is always just less than the K-shell binding energy
stems.explanation: Characteristic x-ray energy is the difference in binding energy of two shells (e.g. BE K-shell minus BE M-shell), so it is always slightly lower than the binding energy of the K-shell from which it was emitted.

keyPoint: Bremsstrahlung production is only ~1% efficient but increases with kVp and target Z, while characteristic x-ray energies are set by shell binding-energy differences.

title: The following actions will improve the spatial resolution of an x-ray image

stems.label: A
stems.text: Decreasing the focal spot size from 1.6mm to 0.6mm
stems.explanation: A smaller focal spot reduces the penumbra around structures, which improves spatial resolution.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Increasing the mA in isolation does not improve resolution; it could only help indirectly by permitting a shorter exposure time to reduce motion blur.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Using an anti-scatter grid with a higher grid ratio
stems.explanation: A higher grid ratio improves contrast by removing scatter but has no effect on spatial resolution.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increasing the amount of added filtration in the beam
stems.explanation: Filtration alters the beam's energy spectrum by preferentially removing low-energy x-rays, affecting contrast and patient dose but not spatial resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Decreasing the patient-to-image receptor distance
stems.explanation: A smaller patient-to-receptor distance reduces geometric unsharpness (penumbra), which is why the receptor is positioned as close as possible to the patient in routine radiography.

keyPoint: Spatial resolution improves with a smaller focal spot and a shorter patient-to-receptor distance; mA, grids and filtration instead affect noise, contrast and dose.

title: Regarding mammography

stems.label: A
stems.text: The tube voltage is typically 25-35kVp
stems.explanation: Low tube voltages are used to promote photoelectric absorption in the breast, maximising image contrast.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The focal spot size is typically 1mm
stems.explanation: Focal spot sizes of about 0.3mm are routinely used to improve spatial resolution.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The source-to-image distance is typically 100cm
stems.explanation: The SID is typically 65cm; mammographic tube output is low (low kVp, lower-Z target), and a longer distance would reduce beam intensity by the inverse-square law and require longer exposures.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Characteristic x-rays must be filtered out of the beam
stems.explanation: K-edge filtration removes high- and low-energy bremsstrahlung, but the characteristic x-rays have exactly the right energy to maximise contrast and are preferentially transmitted.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Screening is justified because breast tissue has a low radiosensitivity
stems.explanation: The breast is radiosensitive; screening is justified because asymptomatic lesions can be detected and treated at fairly low doses, giving a net benefit from the exposure.

keyPoint: Mammography uses 25-35kVp, a 0.3mm focal spot, a 65cm SID and K-edge filtration that transmits the useful characteristic x-rays.

title: Regarding the management of radioactive waste in diagnostic nuclear medicine

stems.label: A
stems.text: Patients administered with Tc99m-labelled tracers are expected to excrete 40% of the administered activity in their urine
stems.explanation: Excretion factors are used to estimate radioactive discharges, and it is assumed that 40% of all Tc-99m administrations enter the hospital sewer.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Radioactive urine from injected patients must be stored in delay tanks for up to 1 week before entering the sewer
stems.explanation: Radioactive urine is discharged directly to the sewer, where it is diluted with non-radioactive waste.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Solid radioactive waste containing Tc99m is typically stored on-site for up to 1 week
stems.explanation: Storage for a week allows the radioactivity to decay to background levels before disposal.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Injected in-patients can only return to another hospital or nursing home if that organisation has a permit for the disposal of radioactive waste
stems.explanation: Hospitals are exempt from needing a permit if they receive only small numbers of injected patients each year.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The MPE is responsible for ensuring that hospitals comply with the conditions of their radioactive waste permit
stems.explanation: The Radioactive Waste Adviser (RWA), not the MPE, is responsible for ensuring compliance with the regulations.

keyPoint: Tc-99m waste management: 40% of activity goes straight to the sewer in urine, solid waste decays on site for about a week, and the RWA oversees permit compliance.

title: In ultrasound examinations, the acoustic impedance of a tissue

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases with the mass density of the tissue
stems.explanation: Denser tissues such as bone have closely packed molecules that resist sound transmission, contributing to higher acoustic impedance.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increases with the speed of propagation of the beam in the tissue
stems.explanation: Sound travels faster through stiffer, less compressible materials, and this stiffness also increases acoustic impedance, so impedance rises with the speed of sound.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Depends on whether the tissue is stationary or moving
stems.explanation: Acoustic impedance is an intrinsic property of the tissue regardless of its state of motion.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is measured in units of decibels (dB)
stems.explanation: Acoustic impedance is measured in rayls; decibels are used to compare relative wave intensities, for instance when quantifying attenuation.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Muscle has a greater acoustic impedance than fat
stems.explanation: Muscle has a slightly higher density than fat, so its acoustic impedance is slightly greater.

keyPoint: Acoustic impedance (measured in rayls) is an intrinsic tissue property equal to density times sound speed, and is slightly higher in muscle than in fat.

title: X-ray production in the x-ray tube (true/false statements)

stems.label: A
stems.text: Most of the electron energy at the anode is converted to Bremsstrahlung radiation.
stems.explanation: Over 99% of the electron energy becomes heat in the anode; only around 1% becomes X-rays, and most of that small fraction is Bremsstrahlung.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing kVp of the x-ray tube will increase the energy of characteristic x-rays produced at the target.
stems.explanation: Characteristic photon energies are fixed by the target atom’s shell binding energies. Raising kVp cannot change them — it only determines whether they are produced at all.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increasing kVp increases both the number and energy of Bremsstrahlung radiation.
stems.explanation: A higher tube potential gives each electron more energy, raising both the maximum photon energy and the number of Bremsstrahlung photons produced.

stems.label: D
stems.text: In diagnostic x-ray energy ranges the electron beam is monoenergetic.
stems.explanation: Electrons accelerated through the same potential arrive at the anode with essentially a single energy (kVp × e). It is the emitted X-ray beam that is polyenergetic.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Collimating the x-ray beam only allows a specific x-ray energy level to pass through to the patient.
stems.explanation: Collimation restricts the geometric extent of the beam, not its energy content. Changing the spectrum is the job of filtration.

keyPoint: In the x-ray tube the electron beam is monoenergetic and ~99% of its energy becomes heat; kVp changes Bremsstrahlung quantity and energy but characteristic x-ray energies are fixed by the target, and collimation shapes the beam area rather than its spectrum.
